usage: Standalone color noun; works as 'purple (one)' in shops
Color + noun = the most common modifier pattern
I'll take the purple one, please
Natural way to pick a color at a store
examples: 색 + 을/를 좋아해요 = stating a favorite
Does this T-shirt also come in purple?
Asking about color options while shopping
Which is better, the purple or the pink?
nuance: 보라색 covers the whole purple range, and 자주색 leans toward a deeper reddish-purple while 연보라색 is the pale lilac you'll see on cosmetics and stationery. In everyday speech most people just say 보라색 for anything purple, so you rarely need the more specific words unless you're matching paint or clothes precisely.
mistakes: Dropping 색 and saying just 보라 — natural in casual speech but 보라색 is the safe full form when naming the color.
Confusing 보라색 (purple) with 파란색 (blue); they're separate colors in Korean, not shades of one word.

usage: The standard word for pink; 핑크 (loanword) is just as common
Do you have a color other than pink?
Asking for alternatives at a shop
examples: The cherry blossoms are pink, so they're really pretty.
이라서 = 'because it is', giving a reason
I painted my daughter's room pink.
Red suits you better than pink.
nuance: Koreans use 분홍색 and the English loanword 핑크 almost interchangeably, with 핑크 sounding a bit trendier in fashion and beauty contexts. There's no negative 'girly' baggage built into the word itself, though pastel 연분홍색 vs bright 형광 핑크 (neon pink) signal very different vibes.
mistakes: Saying 빨간색 for pink — pink is its own color word (분홍색), not 'light red'.
Writing 분홍 without 색 in careful contexts; spoken Korean often shortens it, but 분홍색 is the full color noun.

usage: Everyday word for gray; very common in clothing
Color + clothing item, super common combo
계열 = 'family of colors', used when shopping
examples: 오늘 하늘이 회색이라 비 올 것 같아요.
The sky is gray today, so it looks like it'll rain.
올 것 같아요 = 'looks like it will', a guess
A gray suit is the safest choice.
Which should I buy, gray or black?
ㄹ까요? = asking for an opinion on a decision
nuance: 회색 is the go-to neutral in Korean wardrobes and interiors, often praised as 무난하다 (a safe, fail-proof choice). Shades split into 연회색 (light gray) and 진회색 / 차콜 (charcoal), and you'll hear people describe an overcast mood or 'gray' day with 회색 just like in English.
mistakes: Pronouncing it like two flat syllables; 회 is closer to 'hwe', not 'hoe-ee'.
Mixing up 회색 (gray) with 흰색/하얀색 (white) — gray is its own neutral, not a kind of white.

usage: Standard word for brown (hair, furniture, clothes)
밝은 = bright/light, used for hair dye etc.
examples: 갈색 구두가 이 바지랑 잘 어울려요.
Brown shoes go well with these pants.
랑 잘 어울리다 = goes well with
When you roast coffee beans, they turn brown.
nuance: 갈색 is your all-purpose brown for hair, leather, wood, and coffee, while 밤색 (chestnut) specifically names a warm reddish-brown often used for hair and shoes. For very light tan tones people sometimes borrow 베이지(색) instead, so 갈색 sits in the medium-to-dark part of the brown range.
mistakes: Saying 검은색 for dark brown hair; Koreans distinguish 진갈색 (dark brown) from 검은색 (black).
Using 노란색 for blonde — that's 금발 or 밝은 갈색, not 노란색.

usage: Darker than 파란색; common in suits and uniforms
네이비 is used interchangeably in fashion
계열 = color family, used when matching
examples: A navy suit is a safe choice for an interview.
때는 = 'when it comes to (the time of)'
이 가방 검은색 말고 남색으로 살래요.
I'll buy this bag in navy, not black.
Navy looks more calm/subdued than blue.
nuance: 남색 is the deep, almost ink-blue you see in school uniforms, suits, and denim, and many younger shoppers just say 네이비 in clothing contexts. It reads as more formal and 차분하다 (calm, composed) than bright 파란색, which is why it dominates business and uniform wear.
mistakes: Treating 남색 and 파란색 as the same; 남색 is specifically the dark navy/indigo end.
Confusing 남색 (navy) with 하늘색 (sky blue) — they're opposite ends of the blue range.

usage: Literally 'sky color'; the standard word for light blue
Do you have it in sky blue too?
Asking about a color option at a shop
examples: 이 셔츠 하늘색으로 입으면 시원해 보여요.
If you wear this shirt in sky blue, you'll look cool/refreshing.
색으로 입다 = wear (it) in a color
Sky blue is very popular for baby clothes.
nuance: 하늘색 is the soft, pale blue of a clear sky and is read as fresh, clean, and 시원하다 (cool/refreshing), which is why it's a summer-shirt and baby-clothes favorite. It contrasts sharply with deep 남색 (navy) and even with plain 파란색, which tends to mean a more saturated mid-blue.
mistakes: Calling sky blue 파란색; Koreans clearly separate pale 하늘색 from stronger 파란색.
To describe the actual sky as clear, say 하늘이 맑아요 (sky + clear), not 하늘색이 맑아요 — 하늘색 is the color name, not the sky itself.

usage: Everyday word for a circle (vs. formal 원)
치다 here = mark/put a circle on
examples: 에 동그라미를 치다 = put a circle on
The child drew a circle on the paper.
Circle for correct, X for wrong.
가위표 = the X mark, paired with 동그라미
nuance: 동그라미 is the casual, everyday word for a circle, while 원 is the formal/mathematical term you'd use in geometry class. In Korea a 동그라미 (O) means 'correct' and an X (가위표/엑스) means 'wrong', the reverse of the American check/cross habit, so this comes up constantly when grading or filling forms.
mistakes: Using 원 in casual speech where 동그라미 sounds more natural for an ordinary round shape.
Assuming a circle mark is neutral — in Korea 동그라미 specifically signals 'correct/yes'.

usage: Casual word for a triangle (vs. formal 삼각형)
모양 = shape, attaches to the shape word
examples: I cut the gimbap into triangle shapes.
This sign is a triangle, so it's a warning sign.
Circle if correct, triangle if it's iffy.
nuance: 세모 is the friendly everyday word for a triangle, with 삼각형 reserved for math and formal writing. As a grading mark, 세모 means 'partially correct' or 'so-so', sitting between 동그라미 (correct) and the X — handy to recognize when a teacher or coworker marks up your work.
mistakes: Defaulting to 삼각형 in casual talk; 세모 is what people actually say for a simple triangle.
Spelling it 세모형 — the casual word is just 세모 (the formal one is 삼각형).

usage: Casual word; covers both square and rectangle
네모나다 → 네모난 + noun, e.g. 네모난 상자
칸 = a cell on a form or grid
examples: Write your name inside the box.
It looks nicer served on a square plate.
네모난 + noun; 담다 = to plate/put in
nuance: 네모 casually covers both squares and rectangles; if you need to be precise, 정사각형 is a true square and 직사각형 is a rectangle. The adjective form 네모나다 (→ 네모난) is very common for describing boxy, angular objects, and 네모 칸 is the everyday term for a fill-in box on any form.
mistakes: Assuming 네모 means only a perfect square — colloquially it includes rectangles too.
Forgetting the adjective is 네모나다 (네모난 상자), not 'X 네모적인'.

examples: 저는 무늬 없는 옷보다 줄무늬가 좋아요.
I prefer striped clothes over plain ones.
세로 줄무늬가 키가 커 보이게 해요.
Vertical stripes make you look taller.
커 보이게 하다 = make (you) look taller
nuance: 줄무늬 literally combines 줄 (line) and 무늬 (pattern), and Koreans casually specify 가로 (horizontal) vs 세로 (vertical) stripes when it matters for fashion. The base word 무늬 is the general term for any pattern, so you'll see it recombined in 체크무늬, 물방울무늬, 꽃무늬 (floral), and more.
mistakes: Saying 줄 alone for a striped pattern; the pattern word needs 무늬 (줄무늬).
Mispronouncing 무늬 — it sounds like '무니', not 'mu-nui'.

usage: 패턴 (loanword) is also used in fashion
examples: Plaid shirts suit the fall season well.
I'm thinking of buying a plaid skirt.
nuance: 체크무늬 uses the English loanword 체크 plus native 무늬 and covers everything from gingham to tartan plaid. It's strongly associated with autumn and winter fashion (flannel shirts, scarves) and with cozy homeware like blankets and tablecloths, so the word carries a warm, casual feel.
mistakes: Saying just 체크 for the fabric pattern in careful speech; the full pattern noun is 체크무늬.
Confusing 체크무늬 (the pattern) with 체크(하다) meaning 'to check/verify' something.

usage: 땡땡이 is the colloquial nickname for dots
examples: 귀엽다 = cute, common for this pattern
우산에 물방울무늬가 있어서 비 올 때 잘 어울려요.
The umbrella has polka dots, which suit rainy days well.
These days people also call it 'ttaengttaeng-i' dots a lot.
nuance: 물방울무늬 literally means 'water-drop pattern' and is the textbook word for polka dots, but in casual speech many Koreans say 땡땡이(무늬). The pattern reads as retro and cute (귀엽다), popular on dresses, blouses, and umbrellas, and like other patterns it's built from the base 무늬.
mistakes: Translating polka dots as '점무늬'; the natural words are 물방울무늬 or casual 땡땡이무늬.
Dropping 무늬 and saying only 물방울, which just means a single water drop, not the pattern.
